newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION-South African job creation in low Gear.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-South African job creation in low Gear.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

As one of our financial dailies said, government has at last admitted what everyone outside of government has known for a long time, namely that the promises or expectations of the Government's Employment and Redistribution (Gear) strategy, with regard to employment creation, are not being realised.
Other aspects of Gear, such as current economic growth, investment, and fiscal restraint, are arguably on track.

The major hope of the programme lay with the manufacturing industry, where overtly there has been and there continues to be promise of substantial investments. The growth of manufacturing industry was expected to be accompanied by significant increases in employment opportunities.

Indeed, in the strategy document, manufacturing employment is expected to grow by 2.9 percent per annum through to year 2000 as a result of government's strategy, as opposed to 0.8 percent per annum in its absence. There would be an additional quarter of a million jobs.

On the contrary, during 1996 the statistical evidence points to a loss of employment in the sector, the exact extent being difficult to assess because of the inclusion of the erstwhile TBVC (former homeland) territories from January 1996.

If one were to overlook this addition there would have appeared to be a growth of employment from 1,397 million to 1,429 million, namely of 32,000. This seems to have been the basis of earlier claims by the Minister of Trade and Industry that there was growth of employment in the year and of more recent press articles that there was an expansion, albeit a modest expansion, of employment. However, the addition of some 86,000 from the TBVC actually suggests that there was a decline in employment of the order of 54,000.

And yet there was an expansion of manufacturing between the respective fourth quarters of 1995 and 1996 of 0.8 percent, hardly significant but nevertheless positive. There has been, however, a further burst of manufacturing output in the first quarter of 1997, but this is more than unlikely ?? to have been accompanied by any significant rise in employment.
In this first quarter output grew by 2.2 percent, or at an annualised rate of 9.2 percent. This sharp increase in the first quarter is likely to be reflected in the forthcoming GDP figures.
First quarter GDP figures could well show positive growth in the economy with this performance of the manufacturing industry as a whole offsetting a likely slip-back in agriculture and mining.

The apparent anomaly of manufacturing output growth but declining employment, which of course signifies rising productivity at the macro level by definition, is resolved on closer analysis of the composition of manufacturing output.

The growth has been almost entirely attributable to the respective capital-intensive chemicals industry, dominated by petroleum refining, and basic metals industries, dominated by non-ferrous basic metals, in particular, aluminium producer Alusaf.
The 1990 weights of these industries amounted to 31 percent of total manufacturing, but they provide only 17 percent of total employment in manufacturing.

However, the wood products and furniture industries have also shown positive growth in the last six months, which is at odds with the poor results announced by the furniture stores in the last two weeks. The March statistics, however, indicate a sharp fall off in unfilled orders, which points to a likely fall-back of these industries. They only account for a weight of 3.5 percent.

All other manufacturing together is still below the level of the base year 1990. It has been in a narrow range of 96 percent to 100 percent of the 1990 base for the last two and a half years, although this has been an improvement on its nadir of 90 percent in the third quarter of 1992 during the recession.

What has been happening is that the more labour-intensive industries that are susceptible to international competition and various forms of illicit importation have been held static in their levels of output and have at the same time had to shed labour in order to remain cost competitive.

Meanwhile the considerable volumes of capital formation concentrated in the chemicals and basic metals industries are coming to fruition with powerful contributions to growth of manufacturing output and GDP.

And this is likely to be the pattern of development during the remaining years of Gear given the nature of the identified investment projects collated by the Nedcor Economic Unit. Again there is a heavy concentration in the chemicals and basic metals industries.
In short there is the prospect of jobless manufacturing growth and the hopes of Gear will not materialise as far as employment is concerned.

To quote from a paper I delivered at the recent University of Durban-Westville International Conference, "all the basic policy aspects of the Gear Strategy are either deflationary, destructive of the fabric of industry, worsen the competitiveness of industry, or strengthen the technological trends towards greater capital-intensity. Given this, the outcome for the South African economy projected in Gear is most unlikely to materialise. We are more likely to have a hard-nosed economy oriented towards capital-intensive and high-tech mega enterprises with, sadly, a compounding of our sociological problems and, in particular, an even greater incidence of crime."
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
